Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Portland, Ore. Dec. 8th, 1919 Mr. Hammond, Dear Sir, I am writing regarding my children. I have been sick and not able to be out, but am better now. And feel worried over my children. There is lots of sickness here now. And you are responsible for the children. I ask that you notify me when my children are sick, if they are bad off, I can go down and stay with them until they are better. Also I forbid operations on them, I will not have their tonsils taken out. Should they get sore throat they can use turpentine to rub on the throat that relieves all soreness. I know a lot about nursing and always cared for the children myself. I will not stand for any kind of operations on my children. As soon as I can I will be over to see the children. Respectfully yours, Mrs. Ruth Gilman 351 - East Downing St. Pupil's Name: DeLorme Conroyer REPORT OF PUPIL'S WORK AND STUDY FOR THE MONTH

Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., May 22, 1919 Mrs. Robert Gilman Pendleton, Ore. Dear Madam: Enclosed herewith find Vacation Requests from Edward, Leona, Lorme, Eugene, and George Cornoyer. Please sign the requests and return them to this office immediately so that the children may be able to return home for their vacation, if you desire them to do so. Very respectfully, Superintendent. /MG Enc. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dec. 28, 1918. Mrs. Robert Gilman, 331 Front Street, Portland, Oregon. Dear Madam: In reply to your inquiry of December 20th would advise that your three boys are getting along very nicely. They are in excellent health, and have so far escaped any symptoms of the flu. We have none at school and hope to avoid any recurrence of the epidemic. Regarding the admission of your 13 year old daughter until she can be admitted to Haskell: She will be received at Cushman on regular application which is for an enrollment of not less than three years. I should think you would want your children in the same school to grow up together as brothers and sister should. The boys received their Xmas packages. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Oct. 16, 1918. Mrs. Robert Gilman, Boyd, Oregon, Route 1. Dear Mrs. Gilman: In reply to your inquiry of the 6th instant regarding the chances of having your four children aged 13, 10, 8 and 6 admitted in the Cushman Indian School, would say that I shall be pleased to accept them for the regular enrollment period of three years, with the privilege of course of spending the summer at home with you. Our transportation funds being very limited, you will be required to pay your children's transportation to the Cushman School. I enclose application blanks which you will please fill out and return. Yours very sincerely, Superintendent EHH-S Enrolled Nov. 19, 1918. 5-192a APPLICATION FOR ENROLLMENT IN A NONRESERVATION SCHOOL OF A CHILD ENROLLED AT AN AGENCY. BRIEF. This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or not, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. Applicable laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. Walla Walla 270 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Umatilla Indian School, Pendleton, Oregon. Oct. 13, 1919. Sup't. E. H. Hammond, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: Your letter of October 11th regarding the Cornoyer children is at hand. I am personally acquainted with these children and with their mother. The mother does not belong to this reservation, and I do not know whether she has Indian blood or whether she has not. The father, now deceased, was a Walla Walla Indian of about 1/4 degree Indian, who was allotted. These children are enrolled on our records and all have received tentative allotments, under regular Act of Congress authorizing allotments here. Their father was a full citizen before his death as he had received patent in fee for his allotment. If these children take the status of their father, as citizens, they are not entitled to federal aid in school work. However I am inclined to believe the Department would take the view, since they are now tentative allottees on the Umatilla reservation, that their allotments are held in trust, and that they will be considered as entitled to federal aid for school purposes so long as the government is holding their land in trust. This question was placed before the Commissioner of Indian Affairs a month or two ago and I asked for a decision in view of the recent amendments to Indian school rules. No reply has been received however. It is my opinion that Mrs. Gilman is not able to pay tuition for her children. Yours very truly, [signature] Superintendent Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Oct. 11, 1919 Mr. E. L. Swartzlander, Supt. Umatilla Indian Agency Pendleton, Ore. My dear Mr. Swartzlander: Mrs. Robert Gilman whose last known address was 331 Front Street, Portland, Ore., has enrolled at Cushman DeLorme Joseph Cornoyer, age 9, Walla Walla Tribe, Leona Cornoyer, Age 15, Walla Walla Tribe, Eugene Cornoyer, Age 7, Walla Walla Tribe, Edward Cornoyer, Age 16, Walla Walla Tribe. Mrs. Gilman, who enrolled these children, claims that she is [illegible] Umatilla and that her first husband, Gus Cornoyer, deceased, was a [illegible] Walla Walla Indian. The children were enrolled last year with the understanding that Mrs. Gilman would withdraw them from Cushman to attend public school as soon as she became located. She claims that her husband, Mr. Robert Gilman is a logger and that her place of residence is uncertain. Please advise me regarding the status of these children and as to Mrs. Gilman's ability to pay tuition. Very truly yours, Superintendent. EMH:MG 331 Front St. Portland Ore. Dec 20, 1918. Dear Sir, please let me know how my little boys are getting along. George, DeLorme, and Eugene Lormojes. Respectfully yours, Mrs. Robt Gilman Mr. Smith Please write: Getting along till fine. They are in excellent health and have so far escaped any symptoms of the flu. We have note at school & hope to avoid any recurrence of the epidemic. Regarding the admission of your 13 year old daughter until she can be admitted to Haskell: She will be received at Cushman on regular application which is for an enrolment not less than 6 years. I should think you would want your children together in the same school to grow up together as brothers & sister should. The boys received their Xmas packages. Very sincerely yours, Samuel R 31 Front St. Portland Oregon, Dec 25, 1918, Supt. Cushman School, Dear Sir, Please let me know if my little boys are well and if they got the candy I sent them for Christmas. Also wish to know if you will permit me to send Leona Cornoyer, age 13, here for awhile. I am expecting transportation for her from Haskell as the Supt wrote me he would send it as soon as there was a vacant place. Please answer at once. Kindly yours, Mrs. Robt. Gilman.
